items.d: used to add a contrasting idea (start of sentence + comma)
items.ex: The plan is cheap. However, it will take years.
Although it was raining, we went for a walk.
Despite the rain, we went for a walk.

items.d: used to compare two different facts
items.ex: City life is fast, whereas village life is calm.

items.d: used to give the other side of an argument
items.ex: Cars are convenient. On the other hand, they pollute the air.
The scheme is popular. Moreover, it saves money.
Furthermore, online courses are often cheaper.
In addition, the city plans to build new parks.
The roads are full; therefore, we need better trains.
Prices rose. As a result, sales fell.
Many factories closed; consequently, unemployment rose.
Some jobs, for instance nursing, cannot be done from home.
Sports such as swimming are good for your back.

items.d: used to begin the final paragraph
items.ex: In conclusion, the benefits outweigh the drawbacks.
Overall, the number of visitors increased.
The task was difficult. Nevertheless, she finished it.

items.d: used to show a clear difference
items.ex: In contrast, rural areas saw a decline.
Similarly, older people benefit from regular exercise.
In my opinion, schools should teach cooking.
I agree with this view to some extent.

items.d: standard first line of a formal letter
items.ex: I am writing to complain about the service I received.

items.d: polite formal request in a letter
items.ex: I would be grateful if you could send me a refund.

items.d: letter ending when you don't know the name (Dear Sir or Madam)
items.ex: Yours faithfully, Ali Demir

items.d: letter ending when you know the name (Dear Mr Smith)
items.ex: Yours sincerely, Ali Demir

items.d: informal letter ending to a friend
items.ex: Hope to see you soon. Best wishes, Ali
